source.title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q, let mu: L -> C be the canonical additive character, and for an exponent s coprime to q - 1 define the Weil sums W_{L,s}(a) = sum_{x in L} mu(x^s - a x) for a in L. An exponent s is called singular if W_{L,s}(a) = 0 for some nonzero a in L. Does every exponent s satisfying s ≡ 1 (mod p - 1) become singular whenever |L| > 2? Equivalently, if one forms the q by q matrix whose (y,x)-entry is mu((x - y)^s), must that matrix always have rank strictly less than q - 1?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.1 (Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture, 1976). If |L| > 2 and s ≡ 1 mod p - 1, then s is singular.
Conjecture 2.3 (Helleseth’s 1976 Vanishing Conjecture, restated). Let s ≡ 1 mod p - 1 be an integer coprime to q - 1. The rank of the matrix [μ((x - y)^s)]_{y,x∈L} is less than q - 1.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p with q = |L|, and consider the inverse exponent s = q - 2, so x^s is the multiplicative inverse map on L^×. Prove the Helleseth vanishing conjecture in the special cases p in {2, 3} and s = q - 2, meaning prove without using elliptic-curve theory that there exists some nonzero a in L for which the Weil sum W_{L,s}(a) = sum_{x in L} mu(x^s - a x) vanishes.
accepted.context_brief: Inverse exponent case without elliptic curves

evidence.quote: Problem 1.2. Prove the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for p ∈ {2, 3} and s = q - 2 without using of the theory of elliptic curves.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite extension of F_p such that the degree [L : F_p] is a power of 2. For an invertible exponent s, consider the reduced spectrum of the power permutation x -> x^s, namely the distinct values taken by the Weil sums W_{L,s}(a) = sum_{x in L} mu(x^s - a x) as a ranges over L^×. Can this reduced spectrum ever have exactly three distinct values, or must three-valued spectra be impossible in every such field?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.5 (Helleseth Three-Valued Conjecture, 1976). For any prime p, if [L : F_p] is a power of two, then the spectrum of an invertible exponent is not three-valued.
This conjecture remains open for p > 3.

accepted.question_text: For a finite field L and a map f: L -> L, define the spectrum of f by its Fourier coefficients f̂(a) = sum_{x in L} mu(f(x) - a x). Find necessary and sufficient conditions on f, or on a permutation f, such that for every nonzero scalar b in L^× the map x -> b f(x) has exactly the same spectrum as f.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1 (invariance). Find necessary and sufficient conditions for a map (or permutation) f : L → L to have the property that the spectrum of f is equal to the spectrum of bf for all b ∈ L×.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p and let f(x) = x^s be a power permutation whose exponent satisfies s ≡ 1 (mod p - 1). Aubry and Langevin proved that there exists some a in L^× such that the Fourier coefficient f̂(a) is divisible by 3. Is there an analogous theorem for some prime ℓ different from p, namely a nontrivial divisibility statement modulo ℓ for Fourier coefficients of such power permutations?
accepted.context_brief: Divisibility by primes other than the characteristic

evidence.quote: Theorem 3.3 (Aubry, Langevin, 2013). Let L be a finite field of order q > 2. If f is a power permutation of L of exponent s ≡ 1 mod p - 1, then there is an a ∈ L× such that f̂(a) ≡ 0 mod 3.
Problem 3.4. Is it possible to obtain such a divisibility result involving another prime ℓ ≠ p?

accepted.question_text: Suppose x -> x^s is a power permutation of a finite field L, and call s four-valued when the reduced spectrum of the corresponding Weil sums W_{L,s}(a) on a in L^× has exactly four distinct values. Katz proved that in the three-valued case the exponent must be singular, must satisfy s ≡ 1 (mod p - 1), and has integral spectrum {0, A, B}. Find an analogue of that theorem for four-valued exponents: determine what structural restrictions on s and on the spectrum must hold when the reduced spectrum has exactly four values.
accepted.context_brief: Analogue of the three-valued theorem for four-valued exponents

evidence.quote: Theorem 3.5 (Katz, 2012). If x^s is a three-valued power permutation, then s is singular, s ≡ 1 mod p - 1, and the spectrum {0, A, B} of x^s lies in Z.
Problem 3.6. Find an analogue of Theorem 3.5 for four-valued exponents.

accepted.question_text: Let F(x) = mu(x^s) for an exponent s on a finite field L of order q, and let A_1, ..., A_n be the distinct nonzero values occurring in the spectrum of F. Determine for which exponents s the product of the nonzero spectral values A_1 A_2 ... A_n is divisible by q.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.7 (product). For which s is the product of non-zero spectral values ∏_{i=1}^n A_i of F(x) = μ(x^s) divisible by q?

accepted.question_text: Fix a finite field L and an invertible exponent s. For u, v in L, define N(u,v) to be the number of pairs (x,y) in L^2 satisfying x + y = u and x^s + y^s = v. Call s nice when, as v ranges over L with v ≠ 1, the values N(1,v) take at most three distinct values. Numerical experiments over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 found that every nice exponent s not equivalent to 1 under the relation generated by Frobenius twists s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q - 1) and inversion seems to come from the paradigmatic families described earlier in the paper. Must this always happen for every nice exponent over every prime field?
accepted.context_brief: Classification of nice exponents over prime fields

evidence.quote: Problem 6.7. All nice exponents s not≈ 1 over the prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 were found in the numerical experiment [15], and they all correspond to the paradigmatic examples of Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Is this a general property?

accepted.question_text: Let s be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, with s not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by Frobenius twists and inversion. Suppose s is nice, meaning that the differential multiplicities N(1,v) = #{(x,y) in L^2 : x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v} take at most three values as v varies. Must 2 always occur as one of these differential multiplicities; that is, does there always exist some v for which N(1,v) = 2?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 6.8 (nice exponent). Let s not≈ 1 be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If s is nice, then 2 is a differential multiplicity.

accepted.question_text: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, with s not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by Frobenius twists and inversion. For v in the field, let N(1,v) count pairs (x,y) in L^2 satisfying x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v. Must there always exist some v for which N(1,v) = 2? In other words, is 2 always a differential multiplicity for every such invertible exponent?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 6.9 (optimist). Let s not≈ 1 be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If s is invertible, then 2 is a differential multiplicity.
